The weight is the probability that the system the risk stories are about is a trained policy that has learned some single goal from the training-compatible goal set, the model Krakovna and Kramar 2023 assume (abstract, arxiv-abstracts-2026-09-30.md). This is one of two stories about trained policies; current frontier systems look more like the heuristic picture to me, but goal-like generalization in new situations is reported often enough that a large minority of the mass belongs here. No local copy of the paper beyond its abstract was available; widened accordingly.

Given a trained policy that holds one learned goal and acts for it in new situations, the claim that it selects actions by predicted consequences for a single fixed objective is close to the picture's own content; the gap is that 'acts for a goal' in the paper's model need not mean 'selects actions by predicted consequences', since a goal-pursuing policy can be a reflex rather than a planner. Krakovna and Kramar's theorem (shutdown avoidance is likely for such an agent) needs only the goal, not the planning, which is why the bridge-ps-s2 leaf carries that paper separately.

The weight is the probability that the system is a trained policy with no single objective fixed across the episode: context-dependent heuristics, the reading of Turner 2024 that the picture's Statement adopts (turner-2024-many-arguments-for-ai-x-risk-are-wrong.md L54: the 'RL->reward maximizing' meme). Mechanistic evidence on current models and the policy-gradient point the Turner et al. 2021 closing paragraph itself makes (rewards provide gradients to the parameterization, not an objective the policy maximizes) put much of the mass here; whether this persists for more capable, more agentic systems is the width.

The picture is defined as the case where no single objective is fixed across the episode, so the claim fails in it by construction; the small upper end allows that a system of heuristics can still be well described by a fixed objective at the level of description the two roots need (Bostrom's thesis is about agents 'for a wide range of final goals', not about internal mechanism).

For an explicit planner or an optimal policy of a decision process the assumption is close to definitional, as the residual picture's Notes say (Omohundro 2008 sections 2-3 describe exactly such systems: 'represent their preferences using utility functions whose expectations they try to maximize'). The residual also includes systems of a kind not yet described, which is where the width comes from; note that a trained policy with one learned goal outside the training-compatible set falls here too, since neither trained-policy row covers it.

The two trained-policy rows split one earlier picture by 'has one learned goal from the training-compatible set' against 'has no single objective', so they are exclusive, and the residual catches every other system, so the list is exhaustive by construction. The width is for one awkward case the partition's Statement does not name: a trained policy with a single learned goal that is not in the training-compatible set (a misgeneralized goal) belongs to neither trained-policy row and lands in the residual's 'kind not yet described', which a human may want as its own row; adding it would bump this leaf's version.

As a universal over the systems the informal route is about it has counterexamples, bounded or satisficing objectives, time-limited objectives and objectives that reference the system's own shutdown, which is why it is not higher. Omohundro 2008's abstract scopes the drives to systems not 'explicitly counteracted', and section 1 argues that internal restrictions are circumvented 'unless they are formulated extremely carefully'. Current systems are trained with explicit counter-drives (refusals, corrigibility training), so the first disjunct is mostly false for them and the leaf rests on the second, whether an installed counter-drive binds at high capability; that is the shutdown-problem literature (Soares et al. 2015 on indifference, Thornley's theorems) and the live disagreement of the corrigibility outline, where the author's thesis is that the anti-naturality arguments carry hidden assumptions. I centre a little below one half because the binding question is open rather than settled either way. Attribution: reconstructed, ATTRIBUTION-UNVETTED.

Reading Omohundro 2008 sections 1 to 6 against the four premises, two things are used that the list does not name: that the system is capable enough for the drives to be pursued effectively rather than only preferred, and that 'pursues' means more than a marginal preference (the paper's examples are of systems that 'go to great lengths'). The corrigibility outline's item 1 (agreed by both parties) also records that arguments by example establish the drive only for the example. The paper's own gloss supports the bridge (abstract: 'optimal to seek power by keeping a range of options available'; Turner and Tadepalli 2022 abstract: 'seeks power by keeping options open and staying alive'), and the paper's shutdown discussion (L254) draws the survival reading explicitly. Against it, the paper itself cautions that 'Theorem 6.13 dictates where average-optimal agents tend to end up, but not what actions they tend to take' and exhibits an environment where seeking POWER is a detour (appendix B, fig. 10), and the result is about 'most reward functions' under a symmetry-invariant distribution, while the informal thesis is about agents with a given goal. Author-stated attribution; the reference gap is between a statistical statement over rewards and the thesis's 'wide range of final goals'.

For the informal reading of the theorem to hold one also needs that the environment in question has the symmetry and containment structure of Theorem 6.13's hypotheses (which the setting leaf names) and that the reward function at hand is among the 'most' rather than the exceptions, a step from a measure statement to an instance that the paper leaves to the reader (L252-254 discuss when the structure is present). The paper's own caveat about irregular stochasticity making the similarity requirement hard to satisfy (L260) is the kind of unlisted premise this leaf is for.

Reading judged: the definitional one the discharge tag names. Inside the toy, the agent is by stipulation an optimal policy for a reward drawn from a distribution invariant under the environmental symmetry in a finite fully observable MDP (Turner et al. 2021 section 6, the hypotheses of Theorem 6.13 as stated), so the hypothesis holds of the theorem's agents by definition. Read instead as a claim about any deployed system it would be close to false (the paper's closing paragraph: 'learned policies are rarely optimal'; 'Most real-world tasks are partially observable'), which is why the relaxation lives in the three bridges and not here.

Turner and Tadepalli 2022 (abstract, arxiv-abstracts-2026-09-30.md) state the step themselves: 'many decision-making functions are retargetable, and retargetability is sufficient to cause power-seeking tendencies', with a 'simple and broad' functional criterion covering optimal, random and learning-informed decision-makers; author-stated attribution, peer-reviewed at NeurIPS 2022. The width is the reference question whether 'tendencies' in the paper's orbit-level statistical sense is what 'power-seeking survives the relaxation' means for the chain, and that I read the abstract only, no local copy of the paper being present.

Formalizer-stated attribution. The statement here inherits the paper's qualifier, and the width is the strength of those simplifying assumptions (which I could not read: only the abstract is local) and whether the training-compatible set is the right object for the training procedures actually used, which the next bridge carries.

No proof exists for the step from the training-compatible goal set to the policies actual training procedures produce; Turner et al. 2021's closing paragraph (L260) names suboptimal policies as future work and says 'optimal policies are often qualitatively divorced from the actual policies learned by reinforcement learning', and the toy's first author writes in 2024 that the 'RL->reward maximizing' meme misdirected his hours on the theorems (turner-2024-many-arguments-for-ai-x-risk-are-wrong.md L54). The step has a shape (prove it for gradient-trained policies) and partial empirical support from reported goal-like generalization, which is the upper end. Attribution: reconstructed, ATTRIBUTION-UNVETTED: the quoted sentence is about the author's own effort, and the node's claim that he 'disputes this step' is a reading of it, not his words.

Beyond the toy and the three relaxations, the chain also needs partial observability, non-average-reward objectives and the 'almost similar' RSD sets the paper's closing paragraph lists as open (Turner et al. 2021 L260), and it needs the training-compatible goal set to be the right description of what training instils, which Turner 2024 contests. The three bridges absorb some of this (the first two papers address several items), so the completeness leaf is not very low, but a reader of the closing paragraph finds more than three gaps named.
